```{r, include = FALSE}
options(DT.options = list(pageLength = 5))
```

ariadne integrates multiple biological resources related to various omics
modalities, and thus it is applicable to several scenarios in omics data
science, where the main goal is to enrich analyses with meaningful knowledge
from publicly available resources. This tutorial demonstrates the following
applications of ariadne:

| **Use case** | **Resources** | **Objective** |
|--------------|---------------|---------------|
| Functional annotation | ChocoPhlAn, WoL | Annotate microbial or gene features (UniRef) with sequence-based related functional information (KO, EC, pfam, etc.) |
| Taxonomic translation | OTT, UniProt | Convert taxonomic names and ids across taxonomies (NCBI, SILVA, OTT, etc.) |
| Set enrichment analysis | BugSigDB, GM, GO, MSigDB | Test for enriched or depleted functional sets of features between conditions |
| Pathway enrichment analysis | KEGG, Rhea, WoL | Test for enriched or depleted metabolic pathways linked to features between conditions |
| Knowledge-driven association analysis | KEGG, UniProt | Test previously reported associations between different omics layers (microbes, metabolites, genes, etc.) |

First, we load ariadne and additional libraries used across the tutorial.

```{r lib, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ariadne)
library(anansi)
library(curatedMetagenomicData)
library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(stringr)
library(DT)
```

We also import the ariadne resource graph that will be used to link resources
in the tutorial.

```{r}
# Import resource graph
graph <- ariadne()
```

# Functional annotation

Resources such as ChocoPhlAn and Web of Life (WoL) have been developed to
annotate microbial features and gene families with relevant functional
information, including KEGG Orthogroups (KOs), Pfam domains, enzyme commission
(EC) numbers and Gene Ontology (GO). This allows to derive actionable insight
directly from biological assays.

We import and process the Castro-NallarE_2015 dataset from
[curatedMetagenomicData](https://doi.org/10.18129/B9.bioc.curatedMetagenomicData),
which entails 32 oral cavity microbiome samples from individuals with Chron's
Disease, Type-2 Diabetes and schizophrenia.

```{r}
# Load gene family experiment
genes <- curatedMetagenomicData(
    "Castro-NallarE_2015.gene_families", dryrun = FALSE
)

# Extract experiment from list
genes <- genes[[1]]

# Keep only unstratified gene families
genes <- genes[str_detect(rownames(genes), fixed("|"), negate = TRUE), ]

# Print experiment
genes
```

We search the three shortest pathways connecting UniRef90 to Gut Metabolic
Modules (GMMs). We will choose the first option using the ChocoPhlAn resource.

```{r}
# Search first three paths
searchPath(graph, uniref90 ~ gmm, k = 3)
```
For users familiar with the bioBakery tool HUMAnN, the first step is equivalent
to [humann_regroup_table](https://github.com/biobakery/humann#humann_regroup_table).
However, ariadne automatically concatenates it with previous and subsequent
mappings to return links between the features of interest (e.g., microbes ->
uniref -> ko -> modules).

```{r}
# Weave bindings between taxa and GMMs
uniref2gmm <- weaveComplex(graph, uniref90 ~ gmm, init = rownames(genes))

# Print some results
datatable(uniref2gmm)
```

Alternatively, WoL can be used instead, but only its older version provides
uniref to ko bindings, so we need to import a past release of the resource
graph.

```{r}
# Import past release of the resource graph
graph <- ariadne(versions = list(WoL = "v20April2021"))

# Weave path through WoL
uniref2gmm <- weaveComplex(
    graph,
    uniref90 ~ gmm,
    init = rownames(genes),
    res.name = c("WoL", "GM")
)
```

Then, we incorporate the results in the experiment object and agglomerate it
based on the modules information.

```{r}
# Add modules to experiment side information
genes <- addModules(genes, uniref2gmm, as = "names")

# Agglomerate experiment by modules
mod.se <- agglomerateByModule(
    genes, by = "rows", group = levels(uniref2gmm$gmm.name)
)

# View experiment object
mod.se
```

Finally, the per-sample module loads can be visualised using a heatmap.

```{r}
# Visualise per-sample module abundances
plotHeatmap(mod.se, assay.type = "gene_families")
```

# Taxonomic translation

It 

First, we load the butyrate linkmap from the ariadne package, which contains
microbial features known for butyrate production.

```{r}
# Import butyrate linkmap
data("butyrate", package = "ariadne")

# View butyrate linkmap
datatable(butyrate)
```

We can find the NCBI taxon names starting from the corresponding NCBI taxon ids.

```{r}
# Link taxon ids to names
tax2name <- linkNames(graph, "taxid", ids = butyrate$taxid)

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2name)
```

Reversely, NCBI taxon ids can be derived from the corresponding taxon names,
with the downside that names must be exact.

```{r}
# Link taxon names to ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "taxid", names = butyrate$taxid.name)

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)
```

Alternatively, we can use the resource Open Tree of Life Taxonomy (OTT) to match
taxon names to the corresponding OTT taxon ids using a fuzzy strategy, so that
partial matches are also successful.

```{r}
# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2ott <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = butyrate$taxid.name)

# Map OTT ids to NCBI taxon ids
name2tax <- weavePath(graph, ott.name ~ taxid, init = rev(name2ott))

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)
```

OTT can also be used to link NCBI taxon ids to other taxonomies, such as SILVA,
OTT, etc. We link NCBI taxon ids to the corresponding SILVA ids starting from
the taxon ids found in the butyrate linkmap.

```{r}
# Convert taxid to silva
tax2silva <- weavePath(
    graph,
    taxid ~ silva_ssu,
    init = butyrate$taxid,
    use.names = FALSE
)

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2silva)
```

Using WoL, Greengenes ids can also be translated to NCBI taxon ids.

```{r}
# Convert greengenes to taxid
gg2tax <- weavePath(graph, greengenes ~ taxid)

# View linkmap
datatable(gg2tax)
```

# Set enrichment analysis

Based on prior functional or phenotypic knowledge, it is possible to test
whether sets of related features (e.g., genes, microbes or metabolites) are
enriched or depleted. Common resources for gene and microbe-set enrichment
analyses include MSigDB and BugSigDB, respectively.

Certain sets of interest can be obtained by searching for keywords in their
descriptive names. For example, we can select ADHD-related sets from BugSig
through the ariadne graph.

```{r}
# Retrieve all unique BugSig sets
bugsig2name <- linkNames(graph, "bugsig")

# Extract sets related to ADHD
adhd.sets <- bugsig2name[str_detect(bugsig2name$bugsig.name, fixed("ADHD")), ]

# View sets of interest
datatable(adhd.sets)
```

We load and process the
[Tengeler2020](https://microbiome.github.io/mia/reference/Tengeler2020.html)
experiment, which includes metabolome and microbiome from stool samples of
humanised ADHD mice. 

```{r}
# Import experiment object
data("Tengeler2020", package = "mia")

# Rename experiment object
tse <- Tengeler2020

# Transform counts to relative abundance
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")

# View experiment object
tse
```

The next step is to link the microbial features at the Genus level to their
corresponding OTT taxon ids, which we can use as initial values for the
weave.

```{r}
# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = rowData(tse)$Genus)

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)
```

We weave the pathway from OTT taxon **names** to BugSig sets going through
OTT ids. This way, the output linkmap can be directly linked to the original
experiment.

```{r}
# Weave path from taxname to bugsig
tax2bugsig <- weavePath(graph, ott.name ~ bugsig, init = rev(name2tax))

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2bugsig)
```


```{r warning = FALSE}
# Add modules information to experiment
tse <- addModules(tse, tax2bugsig, key = "Genus", as = "names")

# Limit sets to those found by weave (add support to agglomerateByModule)
adhd.sets <- adhd.sets[adhd.sets$bugsig %in% levels(tax2bugsig$bugsig), ]

# Agglomerate experiment by module
adhd.se <- agglomerateByModule(tse, by = "rows", group = adhd.sets$bugsig.name)

# View results
adhd.se
```

Finally, we can visualise the per-sample set abundance with a heatmap.

```{r}
# Visualise per-sample module abundance
plotHeatmap(adhd.se, assay.type = "relabundance", col.var = "patient_status")
```

# Pathway enrichment analysis

Similar to set enrichment, pathway enrichment analysis tests whether certain
metabolic pathways are enriched or depleted based on how much they are covered
by the observed features (microbes, genes, metabolites). Typical resources
include KEGG and MetaCyc for coprehensive microbial metabolism, or
domain-specific databases such as enviPath (xenochemical biotransformation).

KEGG pathways can be mapped from KOs or ECs, ideally going through KEGG
reactions.

```{r}
# Search paths from ec to kegg pathways
searchPath(graph, ec ~ kegg_path, include = "kegg_rxn", k = 3)
```

We can link ECs to KEGG pathways while specifying a coverage threshold.

```{r}
# Weave path from ec to kegg pathways
ec2path <- weaveComplex(
    graph,
    ec ~ kegg_path,
    include = "kegg_rxn",
    threshold = 0.5
)

# View linkmap
datatable(ec2path)
```

The MetaCyc pathways are provided from WoL2. However, they correspond to
an older version of MetaCyc before it changed to a license scheme.

```{r}
# Search paths from ec to metacyc pathways
searchPath(graph, ec ~ metacyc_path, k = 3)
```

ECs can be linked to related MetaCyc pathways and their corresponding coverage
is estimated.

```{r}
# Weave path from ec to metacyc pathways
ec2path <- weaveComplex(graph, ec ~ metacyc_path)

# View linkmap
datatable(ec2path)
```

# Knowledge-driven association analysis

[anansi](https://doi.org/10.18129/B9.bioc.anansi) provides a way to test
associations between two omics modalities (e.g., microbiome and metabolites)
from the same experiment, while restricting the comparisons to only relevant
or previously reported relations. In this context, ariadne can provide
meaningful links to perform the association analysis.

We load the
[HintikkaXOData](https://microbiome.github.io/mia/reference/HintikkaXOData.html)
experiment, which includes metabolome and microbiome from stool samples of
mice following a low-fat or high-fat diet.

```{r}
# Import dataset
data("HintikkaXOData", package = "mia")

# Rename object
mae <- HintikkaXOData

# View multi-assay experiment
mae
```

We agglomerate the microbiome experiment by Genus and clean the feature names
to find more matches for their corresponding OTT taxon ids.

```{r}
# Agglomerate microbiome experiment by Genus
mae[["microbiota"]] <- agglomerateByRank(mae[["microbiota"]], rank = "Genus")

# Remove rank prefix from taxon names
rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]) <- mae[["microbiota"]] |>
    rownames() |>
    str_remove(fixed("D_5__"))

# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]))

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)
```

We also link the metabolite names to the corresponding KEGG compound ids. In
practice, unmatched entries would need to be manually annotated.

```{r}
# Link metabolite names to KEGG compound ids
name2cpd <- linkNames(graph, "kegg_cpd", names = rownames(mae[["metabolites"]]))

# View linkmap
datatable(name2cpd)
```

Then, we weave the pathway between taxon names and KEGG compound ids.

```{r}
# Weave path from taxon names to KEGG compound ids
tax2cpd <- weavePath(
    graph,
    ott.name ~ kegg_cpd,
    init = rev(name2tax),
    res.name = c("WoL", "KEGG")
)

# Remove KEGG compound id column
tax2cpd$kegg_cpd <- NULL

# Rename linkmap variables
names(tax2cpd) <- c("microbiota", "metabolites")

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2cpd)
```

Then, we create a Web object and pass it to anansi for the association analysis.

```{r}
# Create anansi web object
web <- weaveWeb(mae, microbiota ~ metabolites, link = tax2cpd)

# Perform association analysis
out <- anansi(web)
```

We can visualise the results of association analysis with a forest plot.

```{r}
# Visualise associations
plotAnansi(out)
```
